title: Shared Ancestor in a Search Tree
statement:
You get the root of a binary search tree: for every node, all values in its left subtree are smaller and all values in its right subtree are larger. All values are distinct. You also get two different values p and q, and both are in the tree.

Return the value of their lowest shared ancestor: the deepest node that has both p and q in its subtree. A node counts as being in its own subtree, so if p sits above q, the answer is p.

p may be larger or smaller than q. Trees are written in level order with null for a missing child.

examples.why: Both are below 20 and below 10, but 15 is the lowest node with 12 on one side and 18 on the other.
18 is inside the subtree of 10, and 10 counts as its own ancestor. The answer is p itself.
Here p is the larger value. 40 goes right of 20 and 12 goes left, so they split at the root.

constraints: p ≠ q, and both are values in the tree
The tree is at most 500 levels deep
hints: In a search tree, the value alone tells you whether a node is to the left or right of any other node. Compare p and q with the root.
If both values are smaller than the current node, the shared ancestor is somewhere in the left subtree. Both larger: right subtree. What does it mean if neither is true?
Start at the root. Move left while both are smaller, right while both are larger. The first node where they split (or where one of them equals the node) is the answer.

explain.intuition:
Follow the search paths for p and q from the root. At first they go the same way. The lowest shared ancestor is the last node the two paths have in common, the point where they fork. In an ordinary binary tree you would need to find both paths first. In a search tree you can tell where they fork without searching: at a node with value v, if both p and q are below v, both paths go left; if both are above, both go right.

The moment that stops being true, you are standing at the fork. Either p and q are on different sides of v, or one of them is v and the other is somewhere below. Both cases give the answer v. You only ever walk one path down, so the cost is the height of the tree, and with a loop the extra memory is O(1). It works like routing a URL through a nested route table: two paths share a prefix up to the first segment where they differ.
steps: If both p and q are less than node.val, go to node.left.
Else if both are greater than node.val, go to node.right.
Otherwise they split here, or one of them is this node: return node.val.
Both values are in the tree, so the loop always ends at a node.
pitfalls: Assuming p < q. Write the conditions as "both smaller" and "both larger", so the order of the inputs does not matter (third example).
Using strict tests for the split, like returning only when p < v < q. When one value equals the node, that node is the answer (second example).
Ignoring the ordering and searching both subtrees like in a plain binary tree. It still works, but it visits O(n) nodes instead of one root-to-node path.

solutions.title: Record both search paths, find where they fork
solutions.idea: Search for p and for q from the root, writing down every node passed. The answer is the last node the two lists share.

solutions.title: Walk down until the values split
solutions.idea: Go left while both values are smaller, right while both are larger. The first node where that fails is the fork.

followups: The tree is an ordinary binary tree with no ordering. How do you find the lowest shared ancestor now, and what does it cost?
p or q might be missing from the tree. How do you detect that and return null instead?
